title: Sep 17 Results + Sep 18 Preview: Solid Night, But Those Coinflips Hurt
summary: 5-4 on Sep 17 with strong favorites hitting. Tomorrow we're backing Burns in Cincy.

content.value:
## Sep 17 Results: The Strong Plays Delivered

From a pitcher's perspective, yesterday was a tale of two confidence levels. We went 5-4 overall, but here's what really matters—our high-confidence picks (60%+) went 4-0. Perfect. The losses? All came on virtual coinflips at 50-52%. That's baseball, and I'll take that split every time when the strong plays cash.

## What Worked

The Astros at 63% was the cleanest call of the night. When you've got that kind of pitching edge and home field, good things happen. Same story with the Padres in Coors—we trusted the better arms, and they delivered. The Rays and Angels picks both hit at 61%, validating the model's read on those matchups.

The Sox over the Rangers at 61% was another validation of trusting starting pitching advantage in a hostile road environment.

## The Misses: Coinflip Territory

Look, I'm not losing sleep over going 1-4 on picks between 50-52%. These were essentially tosses where the model saw marginal edges. The Brewers-Pirates game at 52%? That's telling you it's a pick-em. Same with Tigers-Sox at 51%. The Reds and Mets picks both sat at exactly 50%—dead even.

This is where discipline matters. We report what the model sees, even when it's saying 'this one could go either way.' The bankroll damage comes from treating a 50% play like it's a lock. It's not.

## Sep 18 Preview: Chase Burns Gets the Nod

Tomorrow's top pick is the Reds at home against the Cubs. Yeah, it's another 50% play—essentially a coinflip—but here's why I'm interested: Chase Burns on the bump for Cincinnati.

Clay Holmes goes for the Cubs, and while he's been serviceable as a starter after years in the bullpen, Burns has that electric stuff that can dominate when he's on. At Great American Ball Park, it becomes a question of which pitcher can limit damage, and I'm trusting the home arm with the higher upside.

## The Pitcher's Take

Burns has the kind of arm that makes hitters uncomfortable. Holmes has reinvented himself as a starter, but there's always that question of how deep he can go and what happens the third time through the order. 

In a ballpark that rewards contact and punishes mistakes, I'm leaning toward the guy with swing-and-miss stuff. It's not a strong lean—the 50% tells you that—but it's enough for me to back the Reds at home.

The September stretch is all about finding edges where you can. Yesterday we found them in the high-confidence plays. Tomorrow we're trusting a home starter with nasty stuff in what the model sees as a dead even game.

That's how you grind through a season. Trust the process, respect the percentages, and don't chase losses on coinflips.

— Ace
